title: Secure QR-Code Attendance over RPL-Based Low-Power IoT Networks: Security Analysis and Scalability Evaluation in Contiki-NG/Cooja
content: QR-code attendance offers a low-cost way to digitise presence records, yet a visible code alone does not establish that the resulting attendance transaction is fresh, attributable to an authorised participant, or delivered reliably over a constrained network. This paper analyses the security and scalability of QR-code in RPL-based low-power IoT networks using Contiki-NG/Cooja. The proposed architecture models the attendance process after QR-code scanning and combines token validation, attendance-rule checking, and server-side duplicate tracking with an IEEE 802.15.4 low-power communication stack using IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPAN), RPL Lite, Carrier-Sense Multiple Access (CSMA), and the User Datagram Protocol (UDP). The security claim is intentionally limited to the behaviour demonstrated in the experiments. The study evaluates the rejection of exact replayed attendance transactions, while confidentiality, cryptographic source authentication, protection of routing control traffic, and resistance to physical device compromise remain outside the scope of the current implementation. Three recorded network scales (5, 20, and 50 motes) are evaluated using packet delivery ratio (PDR), packet loss, average end-to-end delay, attendance success rate (ASR), and replay rejection. At the largest evaluated scale, PDR is 91.7%, average delay is 37 ms, and ASR is 89.4%. Across all scenarios, 38 of 38 injected replay transactions are rejected; the corresponding two-sided exact 95% binomial confidence interval is 90.75–100%, which avoids interpreting the observed 100% rate as a universal guarantee. Cross-metric analysis shows that the reduction in ASR closely follows the reduction in PDR as the network grows. A formal acceptance predicate and attack-surface analysis clarify why exact replay is rejected and where the baseline remains vulnerable to QR cloning, message modification, node impersonation, routing attacks, and device compromise. The study therefore provides a bounded security and scalability result for an attendance application carried by an RPL low-power network, together with a deployment-oriented path toward authenticated payloads, secure enrolment, routing defence, repeated-run statistics, direct energy measurement, and hardware validation.
